sources.title: Kinematic characteristics of proficient basketball shooters

notes.summary: The ball's path into the rim depends on release height, speed, angle, and distance. Treat a measured entry angle as one clue instead of one perfect target.
positive: Your {value} entry angle looked clean on this shot. Keep that same lift.
That {value} entry angle gave the shot a nice path. Try to repeat it.
action: The ball came in at {value}. Take five close shots and focus on sending it up smoothly.
Your entry angle was {value}. Try five easy reps and match the same lift each time.

notes.summary: A straight shooting line, full arm extension, and a held follow-through make the finish easier to repeat.
positive: Your elbow gets close to full extension. Hold that finish for a beat.
Your arm finishes long here. Keep the follow-through up for one extra second.
action: Your elbow finished at {value}. Try five close shots and freeze the finish a little longer.
Your arm stopped a little early at {value}. Finish tall and hold it for a beat.

notes.summary: A smooth upward delivery coordinates the legs, core, arm, elbow, and wrist instead of forcing one part of the shot.
positive: The release looks smooth enough to build on. Keep the next rep relaxed too.
There is a clean rhythm here. Nice. Try to make the next shot feel the same.
action: Keep the next five reps smooth and easy. Let the whole motion rise together.
Do five relaxed close shots and keep the lift smooth instead of forcing the ball.

notes.summary: Release speed, angle, and position work together. Useful practice compares repeated attempts rather than judging one number by itself.
positive: Your release numbers stayed pretty steady. Nice. Keep chasing that same rhythm.
These releases are matching up well. Keep the routine simple and repeat it.
action: Your {metric} moved around the most. Try five same-spot reps and match the finish.
The biggest change was {metric}. Slow down and repeat five shots from one spot.

notes.summary: Consistency needs repeated attempts. One make or miss is not enough to establish a reliable movement pattern.
action: Only one shot here, so consistency is still a question. Add a few more clips.
One shot is a start, but it cannot show a pattern yet. Add a few more reps.

notes.summary: Shooting power should flow from a balanced base through the knees and hips, then up through the arm and held follow-through.
positive: Your leg-to-arm chain looks connected at release. Keep the same base and finish.
That release has a stable base underneath it. Repeat the same knee dip before adding distance.
action: Start with a small knee dip, drive up, and let the arm finish last. Use five close reps.
Keep your chest stacked over your hips, then hold the wrist finish for one count.

notes.summary: Joint angles and elbow height describe a visible release pattern, but they should be compared with the player's own repeatable shots.
positive: Those joint angles sit in a repeatable release shape. Keep the same elbow path and leg lift.
Your upper and lower body angles line up well here. Repeat the shape instead of chasing a new one.
action: Use the measured joint angle as a cue, not a grade. Match it for five close shots.
Keep the elbow path and knee lift together; do not change both at once.

notes.summary: Shooting distance changes the needed release speed, angle, knee and hip motion, so one angle is not a universal target.
positive: The release numbers fit this clip's distance. Keep the same lift before moving farther out.
That arc and release height give you a useful starting point for this spot.
action: Keep the same release shape at this distance, then add range only when five shots feel easy.
Change distance in small steps; keep the knee dip and release angle moving together.

notes.summary: Single-camera estimates become less dependable when the camera moves, the frame is blurry, or the shooter and rim are hard to see.
positive: ARC still found a useful shot through a rough clip. That is a decent start.
The shot stayed visible enough to review. Nice. Take the exact numbers lightly though.
action: This clip is a little shaky, so keep the next cue simple. Hold your finish and steady the camera if you can.
The footage makes the angles less certain. Use a steadier view, then check the same shot again.
